title: Genomic epidemiology of human parvovirus B19 in Southern Brazil, 2015-2024.
abstract: Human parvovirus B19 (B19V) causes erythema infectiosum and, in severe cases, has been associated with hydrops fetalis and transient aplastic crises. Despite its clinical importance, particularly in vulnerable groups such as pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals, epidemiological and genomic data on B19V remain limited. We investigated 4,118 samples collected from patients with exanthematous illness in Rio Grande do Sul, Southern Brazil, between 2015 and 2024 using serological and molecular testing, and developed an amplicon-based whole-genome sequencing protocol for B19V, generating 47 near-complete genomes. B19V was detected across all age groups, with a higher frequency among females (62.4%), and among adults aged 21-40 years. Viral circulation was detected year-round, with a modest increase in July and a more pronounced peak in September, consistent with Southern Hemisphere winter seasonality. Forty-one genomes from the 46 included in the dated phylogeny clustered in a single well-supported clade containing sequences from other Brazilian states, with Rio Grande do Sul sequences interspersed rather than forming a single lineage derived from one introduction. The remaining five genomes clustered with sequences from other regions of Brazil and Argentina. This phylogenetic pattern reflects sustained endemic circulation through repeated local transmission and is not adequately captured by current genotype-level classification systems. The findings of this study expand the genomic understanding of B19V in South America and provide important insights into its molecular epidemiology, seasonal patterns, and evolutionary history in Southern Brazil.

title: Molecular Detection of Cryptosporidium spp. in Coypu (Myocastor coypus) in China: Genetic Diversity and Zoonotic Potential.
abstract: Cryptosporidium is a globally important enteric pathogen commonly reported in rodents. The coypu (Myocastor coypus) is a large rodent adapted to semi-aquatic environments and is increasingly farmed as a fur-bearing animal. To assess the occurrence and zoonotic potential of Cryptosporidium in farmed coypus across China, a total of 308 faecal samples were collected from seven cities and screened via PCR targeting the small subunit (SSU) rRNA gene. Positive samples were further analysed with nested PCR targeting the 60-kDa glycoprotein (gp60) gene. The overall infection rate was 8.8% (27/308), with city-level prevalence ranging from 0% (0/22) to 19.4% (19/98). Four distinct Cryptosporidium species/genotypes were identified: C. ubiquitum (n = 15), C. myocastoris (n = 5), C. parvum (n = 1), and the Cryptosporidium deer mouse genotype IV (n = 6). Further subtyping classified the C. parvum isolate as IIaA18G1R1 (n = 1) and revealed a novel C. ubiquitum subtype family, designated XIIk (n = 13). Phylogenetically, XIIk clustered with the zoonotic XIIa group. These results reveal the genetic diversity of Cryptosporidium in farmed coypus and highlight the need for further investigation of its zoonotic potential.

title: Lineage-specific and geographic structuring of variants in genes encoding penicillin-binding proteins in
abstract: To characterize the global mutational landscape of genes encoding penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) or β-lactam-interacting proteins in Treponema pallidum (T. pallidum), examine subspecies- and lineage-specific distribution patterns and geographic heterogeneity, and provide a reference for interpreting the potential molecular basis of reduced susceptibility to β-lactam agents. Whole-genome sequences from 737 T. pallidum genomes originating from 40 countries across six continents were analyzed using the Nichols strain (GenBank: CP004010.2) as the reference genome. Nonsynonymous variants were identified in four genes encoding penicillin-binding or β-lactam-interacting proteins: pbp1, pbp2, mrcA, and tp47. Site-level variant frequencies were calculated using site-specific callable denominators after excluding NA calls. Exact mutation-profile analyses were restricted to the 462 genomes callable at all 61 sites. Group differences were evaluated using conditional fixed-margin Monte Carlo tests based on Pearson's χ² statistic, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons; association strength was quantified using Cramér's V. A total of 61 nonsynonymous variant sites were identified. These variants were unevenly distributed and concentrated at a limited number of recurrent sites, with clear subspecies- and lineage-specific patterns. The SS14 lineage was marked by the frequent co-occurrence of pbp1 P564L and tp47 S394R, consistent with a conserved core variant profile. By contrast, mrcA A506T was associated with the Nichols lineage (V = 0.496), whereas tp47 V18A was detected in all callable T. pallidum subsp. pertenue (TPE) and T. pallidum subsp. endemicum (TEN) genomes, consistent with a shared TPE/TEN background-associated difference relative to Nichols (V = 1.000). Among the 462 complete-case genomes, 295 (63.9%) carried exact multiple-variant profiles. Profiles involving three genes were the most common, occurring in 241/462 genomes (52.2%) and predominantly in the SS14 lineage. Geographic analysis of variant-positive genomes showed substantial regional structuring, although these patterns should be interpreted in the context of subspecies and lineage composition. Europe and North America were enriched for a four-site core combination (pbp1 P564L + mrcA G708S + mrcA M625V + tp47 S394R), East Asia showed enrichment of A506V-containing pbp1-mrcA-tp47 three-gene profiles, and Africa and Oceania were characterized mainly by single-site tp47 V18A variants associated with TPE circulation. Genes encoding penicillin-binding or β-lactam-interacting proteins in T. pallidum showed lineage-specific and geographically structured nonsynonymous variation. We propose a core-backbone plus regional-accessory model, in which the SS14 lineage carries a widely distributed conserved core variant profile, whereas regional differences are shaped by additional accessory variants together with subspecies and lineage composition. This framework supports the interpretation of candidate β-lactam-interacting loci in their evolutionary and geographic context and highlights the value of continued global molecular surveillance.IMPORTANCESyphilis caused by Treponema pallidum remains a persistent global public health burden, and emerging reduced susceptibility to β-lactams threatens syphilis treatment and control. This study systematically characterizes global mutational profiles of penicillin-binding and β-lactam-interacting proteins in T. pallidum based on hundreds of worldwide genomes. It reveals distinct lineage-specific and geographically structured variant patterns and proposes a novel evolutionary variation model. These findings fill gaps in the global molecular epidemiology of T. pallidum β-lactam-related mutations and provide critical references for clinical resistance interpretation and targeted global surveillance of syphilis.

title: An integrated One Health methodology to study Rift Valley fever, Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever and brucellosis at the human-livestock-wildlife interface in Uganda.
abstract: Zoonotic diseases pose a significant public health challenge, with most emerging diseases originating from animal populations. In Uganda, Rift Valley fever (RVF), Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF) and brucellosis are endemic, yet critical gaps remain in understanding their transmission dynamics, key vectors and reservoirs, environmental drivers, community knowledge and behaviours and the implementation of One Health policies. The Collaborative One Health Research Initiative on Epidemics-Uganda (COHRIE-Uganda) study developed an integrated, interdisciplinary approach to investigate these diseases across ecologically diverse areas characterised by intense human-livestock-wildlife interaction. The study methodology comprised sequential cross-sectional surveys combining quantitative and qualitative methods, involving community members, livestock, wildlife and vectors across six conservation areas in Uganda. Household surveys and blood sampling were obtained from 3018 individuals and 35 focus group discussions were conducted across 96 villages. 67 in-depth interviews with community leaders and 26 interviews with national policymakers were conducted to evaluate One Health policy implementation. Livestock practices were assessed through farmer questionnaires and blood sampling of 2199 cattle, 343 sheep, 78 pigs and 1582 goats. Invertebrate vector sampling was undertaken of 72,744 mosquitoes and 9273 ticks on livestock hosts with vertebrate host sampling of 612 small mammals. 233 large wildlife were sampled by blood and nasal swabs. Real-time monitoring and detection of zoonotic outbreaks was provided by 127 trained Community One Health Volunteers embedded at each site. COHRIE-Uganda presents a novel interdisciplinary methodology to study zoonotic disease, applying a One Health approach integrating molecular epidemiology, ecology, social sciences and community participatory methods involving humans, livestock, vectors, and wildlife to inform culturally sensitive zoonotic disease interventions.

title: Whole-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis of Anolis adenovirus 2 reveals conserved genome organization and gene-specific evolutionary patterns.
abstract: Adenoviruses, which infect vertebrates, have a rich history of evolution that includes both host switching and coevolution, particularly within Barthadenovirus, a genus that infects squamate reptiles, birds, and mammals. Potential host-switching events can be identified by comparing the evolutionary histories between viruses and their hosts; however, many Barthadenovirus phylogenies have been inferred based on a limited number of easily-amplifiable gene segments. Whole-genome sequencing of novel strains of Barthadenovirus can provide greater phylogenetic confidence, and therefore more accurately identify host-switching when it occurs. Here, we present the coding-complete whole-genome sequence, annotation, reconciled species tree, and molecular evolution analyses of two isolates of Anolis adenovirus 2, a member of Barthadenovirus. Our two isolates of Anolis adenovirus 2 are sister lineages with very high sequence identity. Our results support existing hypotheses regarding the ancestral hosts of Barthadenovirus (squamate reptiles), and proposed host switching events within and between squamate reptiles and other vertebrate classes. We leverage our novel genome annotations to perform comparative synteny analyses, identifying a set of shared genes across Barthadenovirus whose gene order is largely conserved within the genus. Finally, our molecular evolution analyses highlight trends in evolutionary pressures on individual genes: Genes associated with viral replication and structure have experienced slower rates of evolution than those encoding proteins involved in host interaction. Our two sequenced isolates of Anolis adenovirus 2 add to an expanding number of adenovirus genomic resources and facilitate future investigations into the patterns and processes shaping adenovirus diversification.
journal: Infection, genetics and evolution : journal of molecular epidemiology and evolutionary genetics in infectious diseases

title: Co-evolutionary dynamics of defense systems and anti-defense genes in chromosomes and mobile genetic elements of Enterobacteriaceae
abstract: Bacterial defense systems undergo rapid evolutionary changes, yet the specific contributions of the genomic compartment (chromosomal versus mobile genetic element [MGE]) to these dynamics remain unclear. We analyzed 6,907 genomes from 213 species of Enterobacteriaceae using a phylogenetic birth-death model to quantify gain, loss, expansion, and reduction of defense (DEF) and anti-defense (anti-DEF) gene families. We found that DEF turnover differs from the background dynamics of the genomic elements that carry them. Direct comparisons among DEFs further revealed differences in loss and copy-number dynamics across genomic compartments, with the highest rates on chromosomes, intermediate rates on plasmids and ICEs/IMEs, and the lowest rates on prophages, whereas the relative balance between gain and loss and between expansion and reduction remained similar across chromosomes and MGEs. MGE-associated anti-DEFs showed higher loss, expansion, and reduction rates than DEFs, whereas chromosome-associated anti-DEFs showed lower gain rates than DEFs. Finally, we found that gains and losses of DEFs and anti-DEFs were positively correlated across bacterial lineages, with positive associations observed for both matching (that is, antagonistic) and non-matching pairs. Together, these results show that genomic background affects the overall flux of DEFs and anti-DEFs, and that turnover of DEFs and anti-DEFs is evolutionarily coupled across lineages.
